## Model selection 

when you have lots of possible variables, you have to choose which will go in your model 

remember, no model is "true" 

In nested models, you have tests

* you have to be worried about multiple comparisons and "fishing"

In non-nested models, you don't have tests 

* balance goodness of fit with "complexity" 

Is your model too complex? Not complex enough? Am I underfiting or overfitting? Do I have high bias or high variance? Will my model generalize to future datasets? 

## Cross validation

Ideally, you'd build your model based off a data set and then collect more data from same population to test that the model works. That doesn't usually happen, so instead: 

randomly split your data into "training" and "testing" 

* "training" data used to build your model 
* "testing" data used to evaluate out of sample fit 
* exact ratio depends, but 80/20 is a good bet 

Evaluate using root mean squared error in the testing dataset --> low RMSE is indicative of good prediction accuracy (because predicted value is close to observed value, so low number)

Can use to compare candidate models that are all "traditional" 

Comes up a lot in "modern" methods - often built in so you don't even see it 

## Refinements and variations 

Usually repeat the training/testing split using iteration --> indicates whether differences in models are consistent across splits 

Folding partitions data into equally sized subsets 

* one fold used as testing, remaining folds as training
* repeated for each fold as testing 

Jeff doesn't do that as often 

## Prediction as a goal 

Prediction accuracy matters as well as statistical significance (different goal)

* Good models make good predictions that adequately describe the data generating mechanism 
* you lose the p values though 

Use `modelr` package. functions: `add_predictions()`, `add_residuals()`, `rmse()`, `crossv_mc()`

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(modelr)
library(mgcv)
```

```{r}
library(p8105.datasets)

set.seed(1)
```

knitr::opts_chunk$set(

# CV by hand 

## LIDAR data 

```{r}
data("lidar")

lidar_df = 
  lidar |> 
  mutate(
    id = row_number()
  ) |> 
  select(id, everything())

lidar_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = range, y = logratio)) +
  geom_point()
```
Can't use linear regression here - nonlinear! You have to get that non-linearity right. You also can't assume constant variance, it changes across the range. Need to capture that as well 

## Build three models, see which works the best using CV. 

First, build training and testing datasets. 

```{r}
train_df = sample_frac(lidar_df, size = .8) #80% of data for training 

test_df = anti_join(lidar_df, train_df, by = "id") #this gives you leftover bit, this is why you have to add row number/id
```


```{r}
ggplot(train_df, aes(x = range, y = logratio)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_point(data = test_df, color = "red")
```
Looks pretty representative of OG graph, but thinner (20% of data randomly sampled out). The red points added on top show testing dataset 

Fit some models 

Linear model (this won't work well)
```{r}
linear_mod = lm(logratio ~ range, data = train_df)
```

Make a plot
```{r}
train_df |> 
  add_predictions(linear_mod) |> #adds column of predictions to dataset
  ggplot(aes(x = range, y = logratio)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(aes(y = pred), color = "red") #adds line fitted to prediction variable 
```
Bad model! Not complex enough (just a straight line when we clearly need non-linearity) and it's underfitted/high bias 

Try a different model - smooth fit 

```{r}
smooth_mod = gam(logratio ~ s(range), data = train_df) #generative additive model, fits log ratio against smooth function of range. Does assume constant variance, doesn't take that into account - we will fix that when we do bootstrapping 
```

```{r}
train_df |> 
  add_predictions(smooth_mod) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = range, y = logratio)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(aes(y = pred), color = "red") 
```
Looks pretty good - not a ton of bias, fits trend well 

Break this function - making it bad to prove a point (don't do this)
```{r}
wiggly_mod = gam(logratio ~ s(range, k = 30), sp = 10e-6, data = train_df)
```

```{r}
train_df |> 
  add_predictions(wiggly_mod) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = range, y = logratio)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(aes(y = pred), color = "red") 
```
Extra bumps - we probably don't actually need that. probably unbiased, but it will probably change a lot between datasets - high variability and we don't want that. 

Do a model comparison 

Can't do a hypothesis test (because these are unnested models)
```{r}
rmse(linear_mod, test_df) #relatively high prediction error 
rmse(smooth_mod, test_df) #much lower prediction error - the best model 
rmse(wiggly_mod, test_df)
```

# CV using `modelr` 

AKA repeat the above a bunch of times 

```{r}
cv_df = 
  crossv_mc(lidar_df, 100) #plug in df, repeat 100 times. automatically makes training and testing datasets (in 80/20 split), repeats that 100 times. stores all the data in list columns 

cv_df |> 
  pull(train) |> 
  nth(2) |>  #confirm that there is a different 80/20 split every time 
  as_tibble() #can convert to a df anytime 
```

```{r}
cv_df = 
  crossv_mc(lidar_df, 100) |> 
  mutate(
    train = map(train, as_tibble), 
    test = map(test, as_tibble)
  )
```

Let's fit models and get rmses for these 

```{r}
rmse_comp = function(model, dataset){
  
  rmse(model, dataset)
  
}
```

```{r}
cv_df = #apply linear mod to every training dataset, and get rmse for every testing dataset
  cv_df |> 
  mutate(
    linear_fit = map(train, \(df) lm(logratio ~ range, data = df)) #anonymous function - get training df, call it df, fit this linear model to it 
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    rmse_linear = map2(linear_fit, test, rmse_comp) #map across two things (linear model across testing dataset, get rmse)
  )
  
```

Could also skip function and just use rmse to simplify it 
```{r}
cv_df =
  cv_df |> 
  mutate(
    linear_fit = map(train, \(df) lm(logratio ~ range, data = df)),
    smooth_fit = map(train, \(df) gam(logratio ~ s(range), data = df)), 
    wiggly_fit = map(train, \(df) gam(logratio ~ s(range, k = 30), sp = 10e-6, data = df))
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    rmse_linear = map2_dbl(linear_fit, test, rmse), 
    rmse_smooth = map2_dbl(smooth_fit, test, rmse), 
    rmse_wiggly = map2_dbl(wiggly_fit, test, rmse)
  )
```

```{r}
cv_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = rmse_linear)) +
  geom_density()
```

Do some data tidying
```{r}
cv_df |> 
  select(starts_with("rmse_")) |> 
  pivot_longer(
    everything(), 
    names_to = "model",
    names_prefix = "rmse_", 
    values_to = "rmse"
  ) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = model, y = rmse)) +
  geom_violin()
```
Shows that smooth usually works better, and there is less variance 

## Another example: Child growth

```{r}
growth_df = 
  read_csv("data/nepalese_children.csv") |> 
  mutate(
    weight_cp7 = (weight > 7) * (weight - 7) #this is for the piecewise function, build in change point
  )
```

```{r}
growth_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = weight, y = armc)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5)
```
We will look at weight as a predictor of arm circumference. Tails look kind of weird in this plot, we probably can't just use a linear model 

```{r}
linear_fit = lm(armc ~ weight, data = growth_df)

smooth_fit = gam(armc ~ s(weight), data = growth_df)

pwl_fit = lm(armc ~ weight + weight_cp7, data = growth_df)
```

```{r}
growth_df |> 
  add_predictions(linear_fit) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = weight, y = armc)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(aes(y = pred), color = 'red')
```

```{r}
growth_df |> 
  add_predictions(smooth_fit) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = weight, y = armc)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(aes(y = pred), color = 'red')
```

```{r}
growth_df |> 
  add_predictions(pwl_fit) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = weight, y = armc)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(aes(y = pred), color = 'red')
```

```{r}
cv_df = 
  crossv_mc(growth_df, 100) |> 
  mutate(
    train = map(train, as_tibble), 
    test = map(test, as_tibble)
  )
```


```{r}
cv_df =
  cv_df |> 
  mutate(
    linear_fit = map(train, \(df) lm(armc ~ weight, data = df)),
    smooth_fit = map(train, \(df) gam(armc ~ s(weight), data = df)), 
    pwl_fit = map(train, \(df) lm(armc ~ weight + weight_cp7, data = df))
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    rmse_linear = map2_dbl(linear_fit, test, rmse), 
    rmse_smooth = map2_dbl(smooth_fit, test, rmse), 
    rmse_pwl = map2_dbl(pwl_fit, test, rmse)
  )
```

```{r}
cv_df |> 
  select(starts_with("rmse_")) |> 
  pivot_longer(
    everything(), 
    names_to = "model",
    names_prefix = "rmse_", 
    values_to = "rmse"
  ) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = model, y = rmse)) +
  geom_violin()
```
This is the distribution of rmses across models. 

* Thing that is nice about PWL is that it is super easy to interpret - two linear interpretations. strict change point is not biologically plausible (we also chose where it was, just by eyeballing)

* smooth fit looks like best prediction accuracy - but hard to interpret
